clinicalPearls: A rare myeloproliferative neoplasm with sustained mature neutrophilia without significant dysplasia
Splenomegaly and, sometimes, hepatomegaly are common
The majority of cases carry an activating CSF3R mutation, which is a key diagnostic and therapeutic marker
It requires exclusion of reactive neutrophilia and of other myeloid neoplasms, and BCR-ABL1 must be absent
A plasma cell neoplasm can drive a reactive neutrophilia that mimics it, so this must be excluded
CSF3R mutation status can guide targeted therapy with JAK or other kinase inhibitors
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia is a clonal stem cell disorder characterised by proliferation of the neutrophil lineage producing sustained mature neutrophilia. Activating mutations of the colony-stimulating factor 3 receptor gene (CSF3R), most commonly a membrane-proximal mutation, drive downstream JAK-STAT and SRC-family signalling to promote neutrophil production. Unlike a leukaemoid reaction, the neutrophilia is autonomous and clonal, and the marrow shows granulocytic hyperplasia; disease can progress with accelerated or blast phases over time.
additionalDifferentials: Neutrophilia driven by an underlying plasma cell neoplasm
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film showing mature neutrophilia
BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia
Exclusion of a plasma cell neoplasm and reactive causes
redFlags: Rising blasts indicating accelerated or blast phase
Very high white cell count with hyperviscosity
Features suggesting an underlying plasma cell disorder
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and often progressive; prognosis depends on disease phase and response to therapy, with a risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.
pitfalls: Mistaking a leukaemoid reaction or plasma-cell-driven neutrophilia for CNL
Not testing CSF3R, which informs diagnosis and therapy
Missing progression to a blast phase
